messages.content: What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?

message.content:
Lions (Panthera leo) and zebras (Equus quagga) belong to very different branches of the mammalian tree: lions are carnivores (order Carnivora, suborder Feliformia) while zebras are odd‑toed ungulates (order Perissodactyla). Their most recent common ancestor is therefore the last common ancestor of those two orders, which lies deep in the Laurasiatherian lineage.

**Key points**

| Taxonomic level | Group | Approximate age of last common ancestor |
|-----------------|-------|----------------------------------------|
| Order | Carnivora & Perissodactyla | ~70–80 million years ago (late Cretaceous–early Paleogene) |
| Clade | Laurasiatheria (the larger group that contains both orders) | ~70–80 million years ago |
| Mammalian level | Placental mammals (Eutheria) | ~100–120 million years ago |

So, the common ancestor of a lion and a zebra is a small, likely insectivorous mammal that lived roughly 70–80 million years ago, belonging to the Laurasiatherian lineage that gave rise to both carnivores and odd‑toed ungulates.
message.reasoning:
The user asks: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" They want a biological answer. The common ancestor of lion (Panthera leo) and zebra (Equus quagga) would be a common ancestor in the mammalian lineage. Both are mammals, but lions are felids (family Felidae), zebras are equids (family Equidae). They diverged from a common ancestor in the order Carnivora vs Perissodactyla? Actually lions are in order Carnivora, suborder Feliformia. Zebras are in order Perissodactyla (odd-toed ungulates). So their common ancestor would be a more distant mammalian ancestor, perhaps a placental mammal ancestor. The last common ancestor of all placental mammals is the eutherian ancestor. But maybe they want the last common ancestor of the two species: that would be the last common ancestor of the families Felidae and Equidae, which is the last common ancestor of the order Carnivora and Perissodactyla. That would be the last common ancestor of the clade that includes both orders, which is the clade of Laurasiatheria? Actually Carnivora and Perissodactyla are both part of Laurasiatheria. So the last common ancestor of Carnivora and Perissodactyla would be the last common ancestor of Laurasiatheria. That ancestor would be a small mammal that lived around 70-80 million years ago. So the answer: the last common ancestor of lion and zebra is a small, probably insectivorous mammal that lived in the late Cretaceous or early Paleogene, part of Laurasiatheria. But maybe the question expects "the last common ancestor of the two species is the last common ancestor of the order Carnivora and the order Perissodactyla, which is a small mammal that lived about 70 million years ago." Or "the last common ancestor of lion and zebra is the last common ancestor of the clade Laurasiatheria, which existed around 70-80 million years ago." Or "the last common ancestor of lion and zebra is the last common ancestor of all placental mammals, which lived about 100 million years ago." But the more precise answer: the last common ancestor of the two species is the last common ancestor of the families Felidae and Equidae, which is the last common ancestor of the orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla, which is a small mammal that lived around 70-80 million years ago. So answer accordingly.
